items.title: Christian Activist Sues Minnesota City for Putting ‘Price Tag’ on His Constitutional Rights
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: A Christian man from Minnesota was ordered to pay for his free speech rights — and now he's suing.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A Christian man from Minnesota was ordered to pay for his free speech rights — and now he’s suing.

In a lawsuit filed by the Center for American Liberty, Bryan Conwell is accusing officials in Benson of severe First Amendment violations by placing a “price tag” on free speech after Cherie Stielow, now a city council member, forced him to purchase a commercial vendor’s license to practice his constitutionally protected right to free speech at the city’s farmers market, which Stielow facilitates.

“Government officials cannot force Americans to buy a license before they peacefully express their beliefs on public property,” Mark Trammell of the Center for American Liberty said in a statement about the case. “If they can silence Bryan today, they can silence anyone tomorrow.”

According to the legal complaint, Conwell regularly holds pro-life and Gospel-centered placards on public property and waits peacefully and silently, speaking only to those who initiate conversation with him. The suit states the Christian activist “blocks no one, threatens no one, and sells nothing,” adding, “He asks only to be left alone to speak.”

Conwell, according to court documents, initially paid the $20 fee in order to hold his signs on public property during the hours the market was operating. In 2023, when he filled out the form and complied with the financial request, Conwell “was unaware of what his rights were and was simply trying to ensure that he could convey his message,” the complaint states.

The city then allowed Conwell to be present at the market in September and October 2023, but only so long as he remained inside a vendor tent.

At the same time as the dustup with Stielow was underway, another thread of Conwell’s story was unraveling.

In late July 2023, when all this began, the street preacher stood in a grassy area near the farmers market and spoke using a sound amplifier. At about 30 minutes to an hour into his speaking, Police Chief Ian Hodge purportedly told him he was breaking the city’s 50-foot sound ordinance and needed a permit to continue, so Conwell stopped.

Then between Aug. 9 and Oct. 24 of that year, Conwell made four separate trips to city hall, where he repeatedly attempted to apply for and obtain said noise permit. According to court documents, he was seemingly given the runaround by the city clerk, who said she was not aware of any such permit. He was also told the relevant person was unavailable and on more than one occasion was asked for his contact information but received no follow-up communication.

That saga came to an abrupt end on Oct. 24, 2023, when Hodge and the city attorney informed Conwell no such permit existed.

When Conwell returned to Benson on July 9 of this year and was approached yet again by Stielow, who handed him a vendor permit and demanded $20, he declined outright, reminding her — as in 2023 — he was not selling anything and would not be paying to hold a sign and speak peacefully with people on public property. He attempted the same thing on July 16.

Conwell received a trespass citation in both 2026 instances. He now faces up to 90 days in jail and up to $2,000 in fines.

Even one of the officers who cited Conwell purportedly expressed confusion to the preacher over the city’s policy against speech that should be protected by the Constitution.

“To be honest, man, I want clarification, too,” the officer told Conwell, according to court filings. “There are crimes of trespassing and crimes of disorderly conduct, but also you have your First Amendment right, so we’ve got to try to figure that out. … I know what you’re doing, I get it. I’m glad someone is out here doing it.”

items.title: Stunned Finnish Politician Found Guilty Over Christian Beliefs Reacts to Latest Shocking Development
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "I'm praying that it would give a good result."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Finnish Parliament Member Päivi Räsänen has reportedly been denied her electronic travel authorization (ETA), the required permit allowing her to travel to the U.K.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

As CBN News previously reported, Räsänen said the British government revoked the ETA after initially approving it. The shocking purported move came after Finland’s Supreme Court upheld a conviction finding Räsänen was guilty of “making and keeping available to the public a text that insults a group,” the result of a hate speech charge.

The politician and doctor was acquitted on another charge related to a tweet she sent defending traditional marriage, but the guilty verdict surrounds a pamphlet she wrote that detailed a biblical view on marriage.

Räsänen said she applied for the ETA and initially received a positive response in June — but that soon changed.

“Then, just two days before my travel, I got an email from the government of U.K., where they said that my application was canceled because of what I had told about my conviction,” she told CBN News, noting she had to reveal her conviction when applying.

Räsänen said she’s supposed to speak in Northern Ireland next month at a worldwide ministry event about freedom of speech and faith, but that she now doesn’t know how she will get there. She is able to apply for a visa, which would allow her entrance if approved.

“I got to an immigration center here in Finland to give my fingerprints, and I try to get a visa,” she said. “It is a little bit more difficult and more expensive, but I don’t know if it is possible; they will tell in three weeks if I can get it.”

The irony is that Räsänen has traveled many times to the U.K. as a member of the Finnish parliament and as the former minister of the interior.

“So I find it very, very odd that they do not want me to come there,” she said.

Bishop Juhana Pohjola, a faith leader who was also convicted alongside Räsänen over the same pamphlet, reportedly faced the same issue with trying to travel to Australia.

As for the general battle Räsänen has faced, she told CBN News it has been seven years of court trials and chaos.

“It started from a Bible tweet where I took a photo from the Bible and now I’m convicted for publishing and writing this pamphlet, this booklet, ‘Male and Female He Created Them,'” she said. “I got this conviction last March. Before that, I was acquitted for all the charges in two courts, in district court and court of appeal, but now there was a very close vote in [the] Supreme Court, three to two, and I was convicted.”

Rather than lamenting her own situation, the politician worries about the broader implications.

“This really has consequences to the freedom of speech and freedom of faith here in Finland,” she said. “And, especially, I’m worried for many Christians who are now afraid because they have written very similar views — biblical views that I have in this booklet — and they are afraid that they will be in a similar process in the future.”

Räsänen is appealing her case to the European Court of Human Rights, where she hopes to see the Supreme Court verdict overturned.

“I’m praying that it would give a good result,” she said.

items.title: Words That Honor God
items.author: Karen Huang
items.summary: My friend, Alex, a book editor, checked his inbox, anticipating an angry email from an author. He’d been working with a prominent business leader on his manuscript for months. Unexpectedly, the publisher had decided to halt the publication of the book due to company problems. After emailing th
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

My friend, Alex, a book editor, checked his inbox, anticipating an angry email from an author. He’d been working with a prominent business leader on his manuscript for months. Unexpectedly, the publisher had decided to halt the publication of the book due to company problems. After emailing the author the bad news, Alex braced himself.

A week later a reply came. “I didn’t answer right away because I wanted to think first about my words and how to respond,” the author wrote. He expressed disappointment, then calmly stated how he thought the publisher could’ve handled the issue.

The author’s wise, measured response left a deep impression on me. His behavior reflected what the Bible says our communication should be like, especially when we’re angry. The apostle James tells us to keep “a tight rein on [our] tongues” because it’s easy to sin with our words (James 1:26; 3:5−6). We’re to prioritize listening to others so we can understand them, choose our words, and consider whether it’s necessary to get angry (1:19).

Not only does restraint in speech help us to avoid sin and allow the Scriptures to change us (v. 21) but it also reflects who God is to others: “compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love” (Psalm 103:8). Let’s model our loving God with our words—and our silences.

items.title: Living Water of Christ
items.author: Lisa M. Samra
items.summary: As I gazed at the intricate etching Christ and the Woman of Samaria by Dutch artist Rembrandt, two interesting details caught my eye. The first was Jesus’ humble pose—leaning over, with His hand over His heart—as he addressed the Samaritan woman. By depicting Jesus this way, Rembra
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

As I gazed at the intricate etching Christ and the Woman of Samaria by Dutch artist Rembrandt, two interesting details caught my eye. The first was Jesus’ humble pose—leaning over, with His hand over His heart—as he addressed the Samaritan woman. By depicting Jesus this way, Rembrandt captured a significant aspect of the biblical story. Due to centuries of hostilities between the two groups, Jews typically did not associate with Samaritans (John 4:9). Yet Jesus reached out with respect and dignity to a woman considered an outcast, not only because of her ethnicity but also because of her checkered past (vv. 17–18).

Jesus knew the woman’s struggles and offered “living water” (v. 10) to satisfy her deepest need—the gift of cleansing and life-giving grace available through a restored relationship with God.

The second detail that caught my eye was the dark shadow covering the woman’s face, symbolizing her initial struggle to recognize Jesus as the Messiah, or Israel’s promised rescuer. When the woman told Jesus, “I know that Messiah is coming” (v. 25) and He responded, “I am he” (v. 26), her eyes and heart were opened (v. 29). 

As we encounter people who are spiritually thirsty, Jesus’ example reminds me to speak with humility and kindness, praying for God to remove the shadow that “has blinded the minds of unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 4:4) so that they can fully understand Jesus’ life-changing offer of living water.

items.title: Interest in Dumb Phones Is Growing. Are We Finally Rethinking What Smartphones Cost Us?
items.author: Taylor Berry
items.summary: We grew up with a phone that never stopped talking to us. Every app wanted a notch of attention, every red dot demanded a tap, every silence got filled with a buzz in the pocket. That was the deal from middle school on, and for a long time, nobody thought to question it because there…
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

We grew up with a phone that never stopped talking to us. Every app wanted a notch of attention, every red dot demanded a tap, every silence got filled with a buzz in the pocket. That was the deal from middle school on, and for a long time, nobody thought to question it because there was no memory of anything else.

Now a growing number of us are asking for less. Not a better phone: a dumber one.

Google searches for “dumbphones” jumped 89% between 2018 and 2021, according to SEMrush data. The trend hasn’t slowed. From 2021 to 2024, brick phone sales among 18 to 24 year olds surged 148%, while smartphone use in the same age group dropped 12%, according to a study published in the journal Partners Universal Innovative Research Publication. Youth-marketing firm YPulse found Gen Z adults now over-index on interest in acquiring a dumb phone compared to the general population, at 28% versus 26% for millennials.

Academic research backs up what the numbers suggest. A study out of the University of Texas at Austin, published in PNAS Nexus, found that when 467 participants blocked internet access on their smartphones for two weeks, 91% reported meaningfully better mental health and well-being. Their sustained attention improved by an amount researchers compared to reversing roughly a decade of decline. Psychologist Adrian Ward, who led the study, found the results were comparable to those seen with antidepressant treatment.

Some outlets have started calling this shift the “dopamine diet,” a deliberate scaling back of the stimulation smartphones are built to deliver. Melissa DiMartino, associate professor of psychology at the New York Institute of Technology, told Yahoo Life the pull toward a phone works on the brain the same way other habit-forming behaviors do.

“Smartphones have the same chemical reaction in the brain as drugs and alcohol,” DiMartino said.

Digital psychologist Dr. Rachael Kent has observed something similar among the young people making the switch. Kent told Tyla the trend reflects a broader awakening to how much the digital world shapes daily thought, feeling and behavior.

Gabriela Nguyen is one example of that awakening in practice. The 23-year-old Harvard graduate student didn’t set out to build a following. She was trying to finish her homework at 15 when she looked at her phone and felt something closer to betrayal than convenience. The thing meant to connect her to people was sabotaging her focus instead.

For years, she tried moderation. Silencing notifications. Five-minute limits on certain apps. None of it stuck, because the apps are built to make moderation nearly impossible. So she started deleting accounts one at a time, then bought a flip phone to remove any easy way back. By the time she started her master’s program, she was fully off social media, staying in touch through calls, emails and video chats.

“I have stronger relationships now than I ever did when I was constantly connected,” Nguyen said.

She’s since built her experience into a framework called APPstinent, centered on what she calls the 5D Method: decrease, deactivate, delete, downgrade, depart. She didn’t expect anyone else to follow her lead. Instead, classmates at Harvard started asking for advice, and a personal decision grew into a following among high-achieving young adults recognizing the same trap she did.

NYU social psychologist Jonathan Haidt offers a possible explanation for why this generation in particular is pulling back. Haidt, author of “The Anxious Generation,” has argued Gen Z’s brains developed around constant connectivity in a way no prior generation’s did, comparing the effect to tree roots growing around a tombstone. His research points to the swift shift from a play-based to a phone-based childhood as a driver of the broad decline in youth mental health.

Seen against that research, the dumb phone trend looks like a generation recognizing, from the inside, what its own childhood cost it. Gen Z didn’t choose the environment it grew up in. Smartphones and social media were already in place by the time most of Gen Z hit puberty, shaping attention spans and emotional regulation before anyone had a chance to opt out. The flip phone and the deleted Instagram account are among the few opt-outs available now.

Nguyen’s story resonates beyond her own graduating class for that reason. She isn’t nostalgic for a childhood without technology, because she never had one. Once she gave up constant connection, she found more presence and deeper friendships, not less connection overall. Kent’s research points to the same pattern showing up more broadly, an awareness that tools built to hold attention are doing exactly what they were designed to do.

Ward’s study suggests the shift isn’t about abandoning technology altogether. Participants in his research weren’t giving up their phones so much as reclaiming a portion of their attention from them, and the psychological gains showed up within two weeks. Nguyen still uses video chat and email. The dumb phone crowd still buys concert tickets online. The default assumption changing is that more connectivity is automatically better.

For a generation raised to measure its worth in followers and screen time, choosing a device that does less has become a quiet form of resistance.

items.title: Chesterton Prescribes Sanity to Escape Our Modern Monoculture
items.author: Nora Kenney Mittiga
items.summary:
Nora Kenney Mittiga

We must insist upon human particularity over dehumanizing systems, cultivation over manufacture, creation over consumption, and life over the culture of death.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Nora Kenney Mittiga

Last December, in a crystalline “polar vortex,” my husband and I drove to Florida after getting married in Ohio. As we drove along Interstate 75, we remarked on an increasingly common observation: Each town along the highway seemed interchangeable with the last. Starbucks, McDonald’s, Subway, sometimes a Walmart—and then the same businesses repeated one town later. And even those businesses themselves had been stripped of any individuality or quirk. No campy Ronald McDonald statue waving maniacally. No bright red Pizza Huts, the kind that have become internet shorthand for a kitschier, more whimsical version of America. Just sleek box stores in drab “millennial gray.”

Six months later, my husband and I found ourselves in Florida again, this time flying into Fort Myers from LaGuardia and driving the hour southeast to Ave Maria for the 45th annual Chesterton Conference hosted by the Society of Gilbert Keith Chesterton. The destination itself could not have been more distinctive: a town of local businesses organized with great intentionality around a magnificent Catholic church. But the drive to get there felt familiar. As our Uber drove past swamplands being aggressively developed by heavy machinery, beneath a sky eerily pregnant with the lightning of a passing summer storm, we saw more of the same: Dunkin Donuts, Orangetheory Fitness, Tropical Smoothie Cafe. Businesses stripped of any kookiness, given generic corporate names by external marketing consultants. Aside from the palm trees, we may as well have been on Long Island, where we had come from, or in Columbus, Ohio, where I had grown up.

Dale Ahlquist, who heads the conference every year, is, of course, an unmatched, once-in-a-lifetime talent. In his opening address, he introduced the conference’s theme: sanity, as drawn from Chesterton’s 1926 economics book, The Outline of Sanity. For Chesterton—as Ahlquist explained with his characteristic brilliance and comedic timing (no small part of why fans return to these conferences yearly)—sanity is not merely the absence of mental illness but the presence of common sense: the ability to see reality as it is. Marked by four qualities, it includes balance and humility (seeing oneself in proportion to the universe), freedom (liberty ordered by natural law), and happiness (the mirth of a creature delighting in his Creator). 

Chesterton—known to many as “the apostle of common sense”—returned to the theme of sanity often throughout his work. As Ahlquist explained, it is one of his great recurring threads. In The Outline of Sanity, however, he looks at sanity with respect to social reform. He argues repeatedly throughout his work that every modern philosophy that departs from Christianity, taken to its natural conclusion, becomes insane. It will lead not only to madness but to self-destruction—to suicide. Applied to individuals, this is tragic; applied to a society, it’s catastrophic. “A nation is not going mad when it does extravagant things, so long as it does them in an extravagant spirit,” Chesterton writes. (Trump ballroom, anyone?) “But whenever we see things done wildly, but taken tamely, then the State is growing insane.”

And as a state, Ahlquist explained, a century after Chesterton visited our land (during Prohibition, sipping bootleg ales with priests at Notre Dame), we cannot seem to escape a wild set of “-isms.” Ultimately, while each may have attractions at first, they become joyless and suicidal: atheism, materialism, Marxism, Darwinism. Especially feminism, Ahlquist argued. Not only does feminism pit the sexes against each other, violating the beautiful complementarity God intended, but also, it is a myopic framework that precludes motherhood altogether as a category of meaning. It is uncreative in the most literal sense. Its logical conclusion: the profound evil of abortion, the slaying of the most innocent human life.

As far as “-isms” go, socialism and capitalism, the book’s principal subjects, also warrant commentary, Ahlquist explained. They pertain to how a society operates economically—how workers get paid and families buy food—and thus to dignity. Two sides of the same coin, both idolize money, ultimately reflecting materialism. One advocated by a Scottish Calvinist, the other by a German atheist, both also fundamentally clash with Roman Catholicism. In response, Pope Leo XIII wrote Rerum Novarum, insisting that the economy exists to serve the human person—not the other way around. Now we have Pope Leo XIV, the world’s first American pope, who has explicitly invoked his predecessor, arguing that, as in the industrial revolution, the Church has much to say about markets, work, and the human person. There is something fitting about this unfolding as America celebrates her 250th birthday. For all our national imperfections, it’s uplifting that an American pope is inviting the world to consider the dignity that labor deserves. 

On this 250th anniversary of America, Ahlquist exhorted, let’s celebrate an economic framework that reflects this sanity: localism. Unlike socialism and capitalism, Chesterton’s sanest economy is not rooted in power but in place. Goodbye to Arby’s and First Watch. Hello to Snook Inn (a favorite local bar outside of Fort Myers). To the old-world Italian pork store in New Jersey. To the Texas saloon that could exist nowhere else. To the Maryland crab shack with Christmas lights still hanging in July. To the roadside Indiana farmstand selling corn in the blazing August sun. To businesses with charming imperfections bearing unmistakable imprints of the communities that produced them rather than of management consultants. If the modern world has given us monoculture, Chesterton’s answer is glorious particularity: Make America weird again.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

What does that sanity look like in practice? The first talk the next morning sought wisdom from our neighbors up north, of all places. David Beresford, a college professor and Gilbert columnist, delivered a lecture about lessons in sanity from his homeland, Canada. I’ll admit that when I first saw those two topics—Canada and sanity—paired together at a Chesterton conference and filtered through the lens of social reform, I assumed Beresford’s talk would be a cautionary tale—a “what not to do.” In short, I assumed it would be about euthanasia. Canada is, after all, the euthanasia capital of the world. Instead, I was surprised that assisted suicide was not mentioned. Instead, Beresford, a father of seven—with the most humble, understated wit—focused on homesteading, on raising more kids than you can afford, and on the delightful impracticalities of purchasing a farmhouse and pursuing a PhD to study insects, of all things, at the age of thirty-seven, with nine mouths to feed. It was a delightful flouting of pragmatism—a delicious trolling of the type of dowdy mindset that would point out the various inconveniences and fret about 401(k)s. 

The next talk, from Fr. Michael Rennier, was also about having more kids than you can afford—about the multiplication paradox that the womb can contain: A new child seems like he or she will introduce burdens and limits on a family, yet somehow the child ultimately seems to multiply what the family can actually create, achieve, and do (not to mention how much it can love). Rennier—a Catholic priest, Anglican convert, and father of six—spoke from experience, explaining that more than multiplying a family’s capacities, children also enlarge the sacramental imagination, teaching us to encounter reality not as something to be controlled or optimized but as a gift to be received. 

In that enlargement of the sacramental imagination, perhaps a child is also like a novel. The next talk after Rennier’s was about a “novel education”—about the opportunity to self-educate through great literature. Listening to Mark Johnson, it struck me that there are profound connections between a novel and a child. Both are acts of creation rather than manufacture: begotten, not produced. Both take on lives of their own, sometimes delightfully different from what the author (or parents) first imagined. Both are irreducibly particular. Both are expressions of fruitfulness and of hope (indeed, a civilization that ceases to produce children will cease to produce great stories, replacing both with entertainment and consumption). Finally, like a child, a novel cannot be standardized. Johnson’s larger point was that great novels resist the reduction of education to systemization. Against the educational philosophies of, say, John Dewey, they return us to first things—to philosophy, virtue, and the questions that make us human. 

To connect this back to Rennier, perhaps a novel is also like a child with respect to the multiplication paradox. A novel, like a child, appears at first to contradict efficiency. A novel, after all, seems the least straightforward way to learn philosophy or history when one could simply consult the primary sources directly. Yet the detour proves the shortest distance after all. Just as children enlarge a family’s capacities, great novels enlarge readers’ minds. Like the child, the novel does not merely convey information; it multiplies how much the reader can actually absorb. 
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

Of course, when it comes to safeguarding the most sacred stories, the Blessed Mother is the exemplar. The ark of the covenant, she gives birth to the greatest story ever told: to the Logos, the Word incarnate. As Johnson quoted in his talk, “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.” Thus, if Christ is the Word incarnate, then Christianity already unites the concepts of word and child in profound ways. In creating or enjoying stories, songs, novels, plays, and poems—quintessentially Chestertonian pursuits—we participate, however imperfectly, both in God’s creative power and in Mary’s stewardship of the Word. 

But then, the next question becomes: How do we educate our impractical hordes of children in ways that reflect all of this? A talk later that afternoon titled “The Glory of Dirt” from Dan Kerr of St. Martin’s Academy offered insights. Kerr’s talk was ostensibly about soil, but also about education. In fact, he described his address on “soil and sanity” as a “reformed gardener’s guide to education.” His central metaphor was that education is more like gardening than manufacturing. And he spoke of monoculture—not only in farming (the soil in which plants grow) but in childrearing (the cultural soil in which children develop). Good gardeners tend the soil, keeping it rich and diverse. They weed patiently. They harden seedlings gradually against the elements. They do not rush fruit before its season. Above all, they cultivate conditions under which living things can flourish. So too with education. It must honor human particularity and prepare children for worship, wisdom, and virtue. 

Kerr’s reference to monoculture also brought the conference full circle. In terms of businesses and neighborhoods, we are living in a monoculture of Chipotle and Panera, where Columbus feels like Fort Myers feels like Garden City. Our towns increasingly share the same storefronts and even the same service experiences, which are increasingly standardized, shaped less by personality than by corporate procedure. We have lost the cultural equivalent of soil biodiversity. The result is not merely visual and experiential monotony but a homogenization of the environments in which human beings are formed. Thus, localism is needed more than ever. The problem of monoculture is rooted, so to speak, in the soil. Recover it, and the rest may follow. 

Nor was Kerr alone in pointing to the land. Beresford’s reflections on Canadian homesteading, Tim Streiff’s meditations on Adam and Eve tilling the earth, and recurring farming references throughout the conference all suggested similar conclusions. Indeed, it is no coincidence that Ahlquist himself will keynote the Catholic Land Movement’s conference in August. For Chestertonians, homesteading is not simply about growing carrots, raising chickens, or posting sourdough photos on Instagram. It’s an attempt to recover sane soil—for families, children, neighborhoods, and souls. Whether shielding ourselves from the impurities of industrial food, resisting corporate monoculture, protecting education from efficiency logic, nurturing our sacramental imaginations, or recovering our vocations as cultivators, the land provides a school of sanity. 

Of course, if homesteading is to be sustainable for those who pursue it, it must also shape how we spend our money. At the annual Troubadours panel, the inimitable Joseph Pearce made a renewed pitch for Chestertonians to shop local. Never buy Budweiser, he said. Support local brewers instead. Buy produce and meat from farmers’ markets and local butchers. Every dollar spent is a vote, he reminded attendees. The sentiment had come up earlier that evening over dinner, as I sat next to Beresford. Support local, he had said—but this cannot be a top-down project of central planning. It must begin in families. It must be grassroots. 

And the principle of buying local applies just as readily to schools. Pearce argued that parents should invest in grassroots educational institutions—Catholic schools, hybrid academies, homeschooling cooperatives—rather than surrendering their children to increasingly centralized public systems. Just as dollars are votes, so too are enrollment decisions. The culture of death will destroy itself, Pearce reminded attendees; it is suicidal. We don’t have to waste time worrying about its demise. Instead, we must focus on building something to “fill the breach” for when the authoritarians dig their own graves. 

That’s where the Chesterton schools come into play. Americans are lucky to have school choice, recently upheld by high-profile Supreme Court decisions, as Pearce and University of Dallas professor Susan Hanssen both reminded attendees. Later, the remarkably talented Emily de Rotstein shared how the Chesterton Schools Network has grown from a single parent-led academy into an international network of more than 100 schools, providing affordable, rigorous classical education. That extraordinary growth was recently recognized with the 2025 Yass Prize, one of the nation’s most prestigious awards for educational innovation. 

Million-dollar prizes aside, underlying much of the conference chatter was a deeper unease—fitting, perhaps, because of The Outline of Sanity’s subject matter—about economics. This was a repeated theme and, it seems fair to say, an area of mild anxiety for attendees (“mild” because anxiety never actually trumps joy for a Chestertonian, who has “tragedy in his heart and comedy in his head”). We are now in the waning of the ’90s-era Reagan—John Paul II alliance during which many Catholics made peace with capitalism (or in many cases, celebrated it enthusiastically) insofar as it countered communism. They understood the inhumanity of the Soviet experiment, saw how Reagan and John Paul II had aligned to defeat it, and consequently viewed capitalism in a perhaps more flattering light than it might otherwise have enjoyed. (Ave Maria University itself, with its beautiful homages to John Paul II and Mother Teresa scattered throughout the campus, reflects that moment strikingly, and Tom Monaghan is, in many ways, a defining and admirable avatar of its finest impulses.) But that consensus is now fading. Increasingly, capitalism itself is viewed with suspicion—not only by lefties but by many conservatives as well. The Reagan—John Paul II era has given way to a renewed interest in older traditions of Catholic social teaching, especially the thought of Leo XIII and distributism. 

Leo XIII’s Rerum Novarum, for example, surfaced in at least three talks, certainly more than any other encyclical. “Don’t just do something. Stand there,” one presenter joked, expressing the general disgust of the group with a certain idolization of productivity and efficiency that has become so prominent in America. Likewise, there was a call throughout the conference for wonder, wondering, wandering, and for taking time to be inefficient. (Joe Grabowski, the vice president of evangelization for the Chesterton Society, who ran the conference expertly, observed that the more wonders surround us, the easier it is to lose wonder, quoting Chesterton: “The world will never starve for want of wonders; but only for want of wonder.”) Wonder itself being not a means to some higher profit but a telos unto itself, it may not be the most productive posture possible, but it aligns with the project of being a human, of cultivating sacramental imagination, and of approaching God. 

“The coming peril is not Bolshevism,” Pearce warned, quoting Chesterton. “It is standardization by a low standard.” In many ways, that observation captured the entire conference. The threat is not merely political or economic. It is the flattening of human life into monoculture: the standardization of our businesses, schools, neighborhoods, personalities, and imaginations. What is the antidote? For Chesterton—the “Edwardian Socrates,” as Landon Loftin called him—it is not nostalgia but sanity. We must continue to wonder, to wander, and to resist the cult of efficiency. We must recover common sense while defying the reduction of truth into mere pragmatism. We must insist upon human particularity over dehumanizing systems, cultivation over manufacture, creation over consumption, and ultimately life over the culture of death. 

Speaking of life, there is life in death among the communion of saints. Many of the participants of the 45th annual Chesterton Conference and the lay apostolate of the Chesterton Society are working to promote the cheerful Englishman’s cause for sainthood. (Some are championing his wife Frances’s as well!) They speak about it with great solemnity by day and mirthfully by night, at the conference’s famous wine-soaked Afterglows. (Joy is, after all, the “gigantic secret of the Christian.”) As America celebrates its 250th anniversary—and as our first American pope revives the kind of “social reform” articulated in The Outline of Sanity, giving us a reason as great as any for patriotism—Chesterton, the apostle of common sense, remains as alive as ever.

items.title: Monday, July 27, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus describes the transforming power of the kingdom of God by comparing it to a mustard seed and yeast.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Jeremiah 13:1-11

Thus said the Lord to me, “Go and buy yourself a linen loincloth, and put it on your loins, but do not dip it in water.” So I bought a loincloth according to the word of the Lord, and put it on my loins. And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying, “Take the loincloth that you bought and are wearing, and go now to the Euphrates, and hide it there in a cleft of the rock.” So I went, and hid it by the Euphrates, as the Lord commanded me. And after many days the Lord said to me, “Go now to the Euphrates, and take from there the loincloth that I commanded you to hide there.” Then I went to the Euphrates, and dug, and I took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it. But now the loincloth was ruined; it was good for nothing.

Then the word of the Lord came to me: Thus says the Lord: Just so I will ruin the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem. This evil people, who refuse to hear my words, who stubbornly follow their own will and have gone after other gods to serve them and worship them, shall be like this loincloth, which is good for nothing. For as the loincloth clings to one’s loins, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, says the Lord, in order that they might be for me a people, a name, a praise, and a glory. But they would not listen.

Psalm
Deuteronomy 32:18-19, 20, 21

You were unmindful of the Rock that bore you;
    you forgot the God who gave you birth.
The Lord saw it, and was jealous;
    he spurned his sons and daughters.
He said: I will hide my face from them,
    I will see what their end will be;
for they are a perverse generation,
    children in whom there is no faithfulness.
They made me jealous with what is no god,
    provoked me with their idols.
So I will make them jealous with what is no people,
    provoke them with a foolish nation.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 13:31-35

He put before them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that someone took and sowed in his field; it is the smallest of all the seeds, but when it has grown it is the greatest of shrubs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.”

He told them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like yeast that a woman took and mixed in with three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.”

Jesus told the crowds all these things in parables; without a parable he told them nothing. This was to fulfill what had been spoken through the prophet:

“I will open my mouth to speak in parables;
    I will proclaim what has been hidden from the foundation of the world.”

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus describes the transforming power of the kingdom of God by comparing it to a mustard seed and yeast. The Church is the body of Jesus, the living organism that makes present Christ’s mind and will in the world. It is his love made flesh throughout the ages, his hands and feet and eyes and heart.

We are all, through baptism, members of that body, hence organically related to him and to each other. Our purpose is his purpose: to carry the nonviolent and forgiving love of God to a hungry world, to go to the darkest places in search of sinners, to be both judge and bearer of salvation.

The Church’s responsibility is not so much to make itself accessible to the world but rather to transform the world. It is the mustard seed, the leaven. In Augustine’s terms, it is the city of God making its way within the city of man.

When we are most authentically ourselves, embodying the spirit of Jesus—or better, being his body—we are most compelling and convincing. When we make up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ, we exercise our mission properly.
